web_evidence.title: An American Marriage by Tayari Jones | Excerpt
web_evidence.note: A sustained published excerpt presents the prison-period correspondence as first-person letters by Celestial and Roy, confirming that this constitutive epistolary section uses participating narrators.

web_evidence.title: An American Marriage by Tayari Jones
web_evidence.note: Ploughshares maps the whole structure: Roy opens in first person, chapters alternate with Celestial, the middle becomes letters, and Andre later gains a narrative voice; it explicitly says the novel is told through first-person narrations and letters.

web_evidence.title: An American Marriage
web_evidence.note: Kirkus independently describes the character-point-of-view opening, the epistolary middle, and the post-prison return to rotating first person with Andre as an additional voice.

search_log: Searched for the title and author with “excerpt,” “first chapter,” and publisher/author-domain terms; opened the sustained Bookreporter excerpt, while publisher-focused searches did not surface a more useful open Algonquin excerpt.
Searched for “point of view,” “first person,” “narrator,” and alternating narration; opened the whole-book structural accounts from Ploughshares and Kirkus.
Searched for epistolary form, letters, and the Roy/Celestial/Andre voice structure; results consistently described a first-person, multi-narrator novel with a constitutive letter section.
Checked Google Books and a scholarly-journal PDF result; Google Books exposed only catalog copy, and the journal PDF could not be opened, so neither was used as evidence.
person_note: The quote set repeatedly exposes participating “I” narrators, including Roy and Celestial, and the sustained web excerpt identifies several quoted passages as their constitutive prison correspondence. Whole-book structural sources agree that ordinary chapters rotate among Roy, Celestial, and later Andre in first person, while the middle is narrated through first-person letters. These are multiple first-person narrators, so the correct label is FIRST rather than ALTERNATING. Generic “you,” aphorisms, and incidental dialogue were not treated as contrary person evidence. The only material uncertainty is that isolated Goodreads quotations often omit chapter headings and voice labels, but the independently documented structure resolves that attribution problem and reveals no sustained third- or second-person base section.
